query: Equal-atomic NbMoTaW is a single-phase BCC refractory high-entropy alloy with excellent mechanical properties at 1600 °C but very poor room-temperature ductility, while its irradiation resistance has primarily been proposed by first-principles calculations. What intervention could improve its room-temperature ductility without compromising its high-temperature mechanical performance or irradiation resistance? State one hypothesis that identifies the intervention and mechanism, predicts outcomes relative to the untreated NbMoTaW baseline under room-temperature, 1600 °C, and irradiation assessments, defines its boundary conditions, cites supporting prior evidence, and proposes a falsification experiment.

generation.hypothesis: Adding a small amount of aluminum to equiatomic NbMoTaW will induce an inverted dual-phase microstructure—with a continuous ductile BCC matrix and discrete nano‐sized B2 precipitates—that improves room-temperature ductility without degrading the excellent high-temperature strength and irradiation resistance of the original alloy.
generation.material_initial_state: Equiatomic NbMoTaW single-phase BCC refractory high-entropy alloy exhibiting outstanding strength at 1600 °C but poor plasticity at room temperature.
generation.intervention: Microalloy NbMoTaW with a limited Al addition (approximately 5–10 at%) combined with optimized thermal treatments to promote the formation of discrete B2 precipitates.
generation.conditions: The alloy must be processed under controlled thermomechanical conditions (e.g., homogenization and annealing) that encourage precipitation of a minor B2 phase within a continuous BCC matrix. Performance should be assessed at room temperature, at 1600 °C, and under standardized ion irradiation conditions.
generation.structural_mediator: An ‘inverted’ microstructure consisting of a continuous ductile BCC matrix interspersed with discrete, nano-scale B2 precipitates.
generation.mechanism: The addition of Al promotes local ordering during thermal processing to form discrete B2 intermetallic precipitates. These precipitates act to deflect cracks and dissipate local stress concentrations during deformation at room temperature, thereby enhancing ductility. Because the precipitates are finely dispersed and the matrix remains predominantly BCC, the high-temperature yield strength and irradiation resistance are maintained.
generation.predicted_outcome: The Al-alloyed NbMoTaW alloy is expected to demonstrate a significantly higher room-temperature ductility (e.g., increased plastic strain) than the untreated alloy, while maintaining similar yield strength and hardness at 1600 °C and comparable resistance to irradiation-induced damage.
generation.baseline: Untreated equiatomic NbMoTaW single-phase BCC refractory high-entropy alloy.
generation.boundary: The beneficial effect is expected only if Al is added in small amounts (roughly 5–10 at%) and the thermal processing is carefully controlled to avoid excess formation of a continuous or coarse brittle B2 phase. Deviations in Al content or thermal treatment that lead to an overabundance or coarsening of B2 precipitates could compromise high-temperature strength or irradiation performance.
generation.uncertainty: The precise Al content and processing parameters required to achieve the optimal balance remain to be determined experimentally. There is also some uncertainty as to how the introduced phase boundaries interact with defect kinetics under irradiation.

falsification_experiment.design: Prepare two groups of samples: one set of baseline NbMoTaW and a second set with 5–10 at% Al addition. Subject both sets to the same homogenization and annealing treatment to induce the target microstructure. Characterize the microstructure using TEM and XRD to verify the formation of discrete B2 precipitates within a BCC matrix. Conduct tensile tests at room temperature, high-temperature tensile tests at 1600 °C, and standardized ion irradiation tests to assess changes in ductility, yield strength, and irradiation response.
measurements: Irradiation-induced changes in hardness or defect structure
Phase distribution and precipitate size/density (via TEM/XRD)
falsification_experiment.falsification_rule: If the Al-added alloy fails to show a statistically significant improvement in room-temperature ductility (e.g., less than a 20% increase in strain to failure compared to the untreated alloy) or if the high-temperature mechanical strength or irradiation resistance degrades by more than 10% versus the baseline, then the hypothesis is falsified.

cited_evidence.text:
Microstructural Design for Improving Ductility of An Initially Brittle Refractory High Entropy Alloy

Abstract: Typically, refractory high-entropy alloys (RHEAs), comprising a two-phase ordered B2 + BCC microstructure, exhibit extraordinarily high yield strengths, but poor ductility at room temperature, limiting their engineering application. The poor ductility is attributed to the continuous matrix being the ordered B2 phase in these alloys. This paper presents a novel approach to microstructural engineering of RHEAs to form an “inverted” BCC + B2 microstructure with discrete B2 precipitates dispersed within a continuous BCC matrix, resulting in improved room temperature compressive ductility, while maintaining high yield strength at both room and elevated temperature.
